extraction.body: Palo Alto Networks is in advanced talks to acquire Clutch, an AI agent security startup, for roughly $500 million, according to sources familiar with the matter. The deal would value the young company at nearly six times its last funding round valuation of $85 million and marks the latest mega-acquisition in the exploding AI security market. If completed, the purchase would give the enterprise security giant a critical foothold in protecting the autonomous AI agents now flooding corporate networks. Palo Alto Networks is closing in on a roughly $500 million deal to buy Clutch, a startup focused on securing AI agents, according to multiple sources with knowledge of the negotiations. The talks come as enterprise security vendors scramble to address the security risks posed by autonomous AI systems now being deployed across corporate environments. Clutch was last valued at just $85 million, meaning Palo Alto is willing to pay nearly six times that figure to acquire the technology. The startup, backed by Lightspeed Venture Partners and SignalFire, has built a platform specifically designed to monitor and secure AI agents - the autonomous software systems that can take actions, access data, and make decisions without human oversight. As companies rush to deploy these agents for everything from customer service to code generation, the security implications have become impossible to ignore. The deal talks reveal how quickly AI agent security has transformed from a niche concern into a must-have capability for enterprise security platforms. Just days ago, CrowdStrike dropped $500M on AI security duo Fiddler AI and Dreadnode in a double acquisition targeting the exact same market. Palo Alto Networks has been methodically building its AI security portfolio through a combination of internal development and strategic acquisitions. The company's existing platform already includes some AI-focused security tools, but Clutch would bring specialized capabilities for monitoring AI agent behavior, detecting anomalies, and preventing autonomous systems from accessing sensitive data or taking unauthorized actions. The valuation jump reflects both Clutch's technology and the broader market dynamics. Venture investors have poured billions into AI security startups over the past year, with companies like Armadin - founded by former FireEye CEO Kevin Mandia - raising $255.5M at a $2.5B valuation to build AI agent swarms for enterprise security. Even Nvidia has entered the space, launching an open agent safety platform that provides full-stack governance for AI systems. For Palo Alto Networks, the acquisition would address a critical gap in its product lineup at a moment when customers are demanding comprehensive AI security solutions. The company competes directly with CrowdStrike, Fortinet, and other security vendors who are all racing to offer end-to-end protection for AI deployments. Losing ground in this emerging category could mean losing access to the next generation of enterprise security budgets. Lightspeed and SignalFire, Clutch's primary backers, stand to see substantial returns if the deal closes at the reported $500 million figure. Both firms have been active investors in the AI security space, betting early that protecting autonomous systems would become a major enterprise priority. The rapid exit timeline - Clutch is still a relatively young company - suggests just how urgent the need has become for established security vendors to acquire rather than build these capabilities. The deal structure and timeline remain fluid, and there's no guarantee the talks will result in a completed transaction. But the momentum is clear: enterprise security is being rebuilt around AI, and the companies that can't secure autonomous agents risk becoming irrelevant. Palo Alto Networks appears determined not to let that happen, even if it means paying a significant premium for a startup that was valued at a fraction of the purchase price just months ago. Early AI security concerns focused on model vulnerabilities, data poisoning, and prompt injection attacks. But as companies move from chatbots to autonomous agents that can access systems, move data, and take actions on behalf of users, the security model has to evolve. Clutch's technology addresses this next phase, providing the guardrails enterprises need to deploy AI agents without creating massive new attack surfaces. Palo Alto Networks' pursuit of Clutch at a 6x valuation premium signals that AI agent security has moved from emerging concern to existential priority for enterprise security vendors. With CrowdStrike, Nvidia, and now Palo Alto all making aggressive moves in this space within weeks of each other, the message to enterprises is clear: autonomous AI systems require fundamentally new security approaches, and the companies that provide them will command premium valuations. As AI agents proliferate across corporate networks, expect more acquisitions, more funding rounds, and more competition for the startups building the guardrails that make autonomous AI safe for enterprise deployment.

extraction.body: Massive new data centers are the physical foundation for tech companies’ hopes and dreams for AI. But the rush to expand warehouses full of energy-hungry servers has also kicked up fights across the world over their impact on power grids, utility bills, nearby communities, and the environment. Data centers were a major bipartisan issue ahead of the 2026 midterms, and voters largely opposed data center expansion at the polls. Tech giants like OpenAI and Amazon are promising to work more closely with local communities and cover their data center energy costs. But following the election, Democratic leaders are calling for further data center restrictions and slowdowns that the AI companies will have to grapple with. From audacious plans about data centers into space, heated local battles over buildouts, and potential environmental impacts, here’s The Verge’s news, coverage, and reporting surrounding data centers and the companies that are building them.

extraction.body: HARRISBURG, Pa. – After a campaign season filled with outrage against artificial intelligence data centers , the midterm elections ushered in a wave of Democrats pledging to clamp down on the energy-hungry behemoths. A tougher regulatory environment for AI giants and data center developers is expected to follow, even if President Donald Trump — perhaps the industry’s biggest champion — stalls any federal crackdown. Data center regulation itself was not on most midterm ballots, and it wasn't among the top issues for most voters. But hard-line stances against the server warehouses were woven into the platforms of many candidates, including the Democrats who upended longtime Republican control of the governorships in Texas, Ohio, Georgia, Nevada and Iowa, many of which are data center hot spots. Skepticism of data centers, and their impact on electricity prices , often blended with the fight for affordability — a key campaign talking point for Democrats. In Texas, Clayton Tucker, the first Democrat elected state agriculture commissioner since 1986, said his pledge to fight data center development was critical to his victory. Everywhere he went, he said, ranchers worried that data centers posed an existential threat to their dwindling water supplies. “You know, there’s an old saying around here that ‘whiskey’s for drinking and water’s for fighting,’” Tucker told The Associated Press. “And that’s exactly what happened.” Data centers were a persistent bogeyman in attack ads According to data from AdImpact, campaigns large and small spent more than $380 million on television ads mentioning data centers. Democrats outspent Republicans on the topic by a more than 3-to-1 ratio. Sweeping wins by Democrats could have far-reaching implications for data centers. Besides taking control of Congress, Democrats flipped at least five governors’ offices and took full control of state governments in six more states: Arizona, Wisconsin, Minnesota, Pennsylvania, Nevada and Michigan. Data Center Watch, a project of AI security consultancy 10a Labs, said it tracked winning candidates for Congress and governorships and found the vast majority had expressed support for stronger regulation or even a moratorium. Among governors, 32 of the 34 victorious candidates in races where AP called a winner support stronger regulation or restrictions. Twelve of the 34 support bans or moratoriums, it said. During the campaign, Wisconsin Gov.-elect David Crowley, a Democrat, changed his position under pressure from his Republican opponent to take a harder line against data centers. Initially opposed to any moratorium, Crowley later said he supported one as well as abolishing the state’s sales tax exemption for data center operators and developers. In an interview Thursday with AP, Crowley said he’s having discussions now about what he'll propose once he takes office. AI giant OpenAI published a framework Thursday enumerating new commitments to the communities where it develops data centers. The company said it was asking federal, state and local policymakers to write “clear rules for how the industry builds.” “Lawmakers should establish rules to advance responsible investment, protect residents, and ensure that the benefits of AI infrastructure are broadly shared,” the post said. An industry association, the Data Center Coalition, echoed the sentiment that developers need to keep trying to build trust with public officials and communities. A coalition official, Dan Diorio, said the industry is aware many midterm winners have vowed to impose a moratorium. “We should expect them to want to deliver on those promises, but there are going to be real-world consequences of that,” Diorio said in an interview. Those consequences, Diorio said, could include host communities missing out on tax revenue or payments from tech companies. Data centers are also driving a broader economic expansion that encourages investment in domestic manufacturing, he said. Wall Street sees red lights ahead after the election AI data center construction is driving much of the U.S. economy’s growth , and any slowdown could have a broader chilling effect. In an analyst report, Morgan Stanley said decisive results for Democrats carry "greater expectations for data center restrictions" that, under new state regulations, could “split the country into areas that are open to new data centers and those without.” It singled out Texas' election of Democrat Gina Hinojosa for governor as the “most important election result" for data center development. Hinojosa has said she’d block a permit for a data center if it wasn’t a good deal for Texans or residents hadn’t gotten a say in the matter. She defeated Republican Gov. Greg Abbott, who had touted Texas as "the epicenter of AI development” before trying to clamp down on it late in the campaign. Morgan Stanley also said Ohio's election of Democrat Dr. Amy Acton as governor “creates significant risk of data center project delays in the state.” Acton has pledged to block a data center project unless it meets certain standards. Local elections didn’t go well for data centers, either Voters in local referendums cast ballots overwhelmingly in favor of restricting data centers, according to an analysis by polling and data science firm Redbud Consulting. Redbud tracked 47 referendums in 44 municipalities in 12 states, including 21 in Ohio alone, eight in Maine, seven in Illinois and four in Kansas. Restrictions were approved in 44 of the 45 elections where counting was complete, Redbud reported. Most voters don't want a data center built near them Support was higher in some traditionally red states, including Wyoming, West Virginia, Louisiana and Mississippi. In Texas, voters in the Senate race were similarly likely to say they oppose a new data center being built in their community. Despite voters’ deep opposition to data centers near them, The AP Voter Poll suggests it was not a particularly motivating issue in this election. About one-quarter of U.S. voters said AI data centers were “crucial” to their vote for Congress, which is well below the shares that said government corruption or the cost of living were highly important to their vote. Texas is poised to overtake northern Virginia as the largest global data center market by 2030, according to a report by commercial real estate giant JLL. In the campaign, Hinojosa aggressively attacked Abbott as having rolled out the welcome mat for data centers. Stephen Sanders, a Republican who co-founded a data center protest group in Lubbock, said Texans were especially attuned to the issue because of talk that data centers pose a threat to their electricity and water in the drought-stricken state. “I would say data centers were on the ballot,” Sanders said.

extraction.body: AI data centers were a major factor for over half of voters in the 2026 midterm elections. While they were not the most crucial issue, voters made their opinions on data centers clear.Big majorities nationally and in all the Senate battlegrounds opposed having one built in their community, according to CBS News exit polls. This opposition benefited Democratic candidates — most who opposed data centers backed Democrats. But most self-identified Republicans also expressed their resistance to having a new data center in their area too — even as they predominantly voted for Republican candidates. Views about data centers are connected to voters' views about AI more broadly. Those who see AI doing more harm than good (which is most voters) are opposed to data centers in their community. Voters who think AI will help society are more open to having one. Candidates like Democratic Sen.-elect Sherrod Brown in Ohio and Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa in Texas, among others, made data centers a central part of their campaigns. Here are voters' views on data centers in selected states. In each, there was majority opposition to new data centers across urban, suburban and rural areas. CBS News polling conducted earlier this year found public skepticism about having a data center in their area fueled by perceived negative impacts on the environment and resources. More did, however, think that data centers could be good, rather than bad, for local tax revenue.The CBS News exit poll interviewed thousands of voters across the country at polling locations on Election Day and in the weeks leading up to Election Day.

extraction.body: Americans are increasingly concerned about AI and data centers, and the impact of computing on climate change. A September poll by the Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research and the Energy Policy Institute at the University of Chicago found that 53% are extremely or very concerned about the environmental impacts of AI—and that the majority of both Democrats and Republicans support policies including requiring data centers to use clean energy and pay for grid upgrades. We asked leading expert Andrew Chien to answer commonly asked questions about data centers. Chien is the William Eckhardt Distinguished Service Professor of Computer Science at UChicago. Before joining the University in 2011, he served for five years as the vice president of research at Intel Corporation. Since 2015, he and his research team have studied how to make computing more sustainable and grid-friendly. In the simplest terms, a data center is a room or building that’s full of computers. This can be a single room, a little building on the corner, or a few floors of a skyscraper, all the way up to huge, multi-acre complexes. When people ask this, I explain by saying, “Data centers are where the Internet lives.” All the cloud computing and the data we use—your pictures, your social media and now AI chatbots—those are all supported by data centers. The difference now is that AI-based services require massive amounts of power. When you used to type something into Google, it would search a copy of the internet. Now, when you ask a chatbot or an AI agent something, it literally performs a supercomputer-class numerical computation in order to figure out how to tell you that stuff. (It’s approximately a teraflop. That’s not quite the supercomputer of today—it’s a supercomputer of a few years ago—but it’s a gigantic amount of computation.) So as data centers consume power, they heat up, and they need to cool themselves; basically you are rejecting heat into the atmosphere. One of the most efficient ways to do this is to spray water into the air—when I was a child they called this “Texas air-conditioning,” but it’s technically called evaporative cooling. Several companies, with the notable exception of Google, have said they won’t build new data centers with this method. But there’s still this huge existing fleet of data centers using this technology. It could certainly be retrofitted. But, companies are not racing to do that because of the cost involved. Data centers come in all different sizes. The biggest are massive 10-gigawatt data centers. The vast majority are much smaller—most of them are tens or hundreds of megawatts. Overall, the growth has taken off exponentially. As of 2025, data centers consume 5% of all the power generation in the U.S. Our calculations show that by 2030, it will be 15%. By 2040, it will be 50%. And we believe that’s a conservative estimate. Yes. Our research group has studied this and shown multiple ways to reduce the impact of data centers. One important way is called “data center flexibility.” You increase the data center’s power usage (by running more computations or perhaps charging local batteries) when there is less demand on the electric grid, or when there is excess renewable energy being generated by solar or wind. This reduces the impact of data centers on the grid at peak overall usage times, which is a major driver for the cost of power and infrastructure. We also pioneered an approach we call “Middlebox.” The idea is to build a little energy station next to the data center. This means the data center itself gets highly reliable power (and doesn’t have to be flexible about when it runs computations). The combined data center + power station can also now actually reduce peak loads overall on the grid, in addition to supporting renewable energy by increasing consumption when there is excess energy from wind or solar. Remarkably, we did a study on this and showed that in the majority of cases, the data center companies would actually make money from doing this, because they can get better prices for energy and they don’t get charged extra for drawing power during peak usage times. So technically and economically, it’s absolutely clear that this is the right thing to do. All the technology is there. But the companies are not taking these steps. In fact, several of them are bringing lawsuits against attempts to regulate them. One thing to keep in mind is that data centers don’t employ a lot of people, relative to say, an automotive factory, or even a store of similar square footage. Once the initial construction is done, communities often see very little positive economic impact. One of the problems is that large data center companies have been pursuing aggressive business tactics. But they do so at the cost of alienating the local community and causing a backlash. For example, a common tactic is to come into a small town or county and tell the mayor, “We want to build a data center,” and the first thing they do is make the mayor sign a non-disclosure agreement about the discussions. When the deal is done, then the citizens hear about it—often with surprise and dismay. Worse, some of these deals carry NDAs into their operating stage—where the concessions or permits granted may not be known for many years—or ever. I think it’s a good idea to ban companies requesting or public officials signing such NDAs and require all such deals to be shared openly. This would decrease the information and power asymmetry, and force the data center companies to compete for community support! Data centers don’t have to be built next door. With the modern fiber-optic internet, communication can travel across the country in less than 15 milliseconds. So, data centers don’t have to be anyplace that people don’t want them. They can be anywhere in the USA and serve AI to the entire population, businesses, etc. National and state government needs to organize infrastructure for data centers. Coordinated regulation is needed because the companies are so powerful. It should be organized and planned to concentrate the data centers in “industrial” areas with power and networking infrastructure. If it’s zoned properly, it will reduce the impact on local community. Further, data center companies should REALLY cover the cost of new infrastructure—for its full lifetime of 15 to 30 years. They have plenty of profit. If it’s really that important that data centers be built, let’s solve the problem in a way that works for everybody. I think sometimes people feel that governments can’t force companies to change. But I don’t really believe that’s true. When I was at Intel, my experience was that if public policy changes, the companies change. The auto companies complied with the Inflation reduction act quickly. American tech companies comply with European policies in order to sell there. We should expect that companies will fight every step of the way to get more profit, but I still believe people can win that battle in the U.S. to reach a balanced solution where we can have the AI computing power we need, but the communities that host data centers get valuable training, community contribution, and good jobs. I think it’s a good idea to ban companies requesting or public officials signing such NDAs and require all such deals to be shared openly. This would decrease the information and power asymmetry, and force the data center companies to compete for community support!

Data centers don’t have to be built next door. With the modern fiber-optic internet, communication can travel across the country in less than 15 milliseconds. So, data centers don’t have to be anyplace that people don’t want them. They can be anywhere in the USA and serve AI to the entire population, businesses, etc.

National and state government needs to organize infrastructure for data centers. Coordinated regulation is needed because the companies are so powerful. It should be organized and planned to concentrate the data centers in “industrial” areas with power and networking infrastructure. If it’s zoned properly, it will reduce the impact on local community.

Further, data center companies should REALLY cover the cost of new infrastructure—for its full lifetime of 15 to 30 years. They have plenty of profit. If it’s really that important that data centers be built, let’s solve the problem in a way that works for everybody.

I think sometimes people feel that governments can’t force companies to change. But I don’t really believe that’s true. When I was at Intel, my experience was that if public policy changes, the companies change. The auto companies complied with the Inflation reduction act quickly. American tech companies comply with European policies in order to sell there.

We should expect that companies will fight every step of the way to get more profit, but I still believe people can win that battle in the U.S. to reach a balanced solution where we can have the AI computing power we need, but the communities that host data centers get valuable training, community contribution, and good jobs.

extraction.body: Massive new data centers are the physical foundation for tech companies’ hopes and dreams for AI. But the rush to expand warehouses full of energy-hungry servers has also kicked up fights across the world over their impact on power grids, utility bills, nearby communities, and the environment. Data centers were a major bipartisan issue ahead of the 2026 midterms, and voters largely opposed data center expansion at the polls. Tech giants like OpenAI and Amazon are promising to work more closely with local communities and cover their data center energy costs. But following the election, Democratic leaders are calling for further data center restrictions and slowdowns that the AI companies will have to grapple with. From audacious plans about data centers into space, heated local battles over buildouts, and potential environmental impacts, here’s The Verge’s news, coverage, and reporting surrounding data centers and the companies that are building them.

extraction.body: HARRISBURG, Pa. – After a campaign season filled with outrage against artificial intelligence data centers , the midterm elections ushered in a wave of Democrats pledging to clamp down on the energy-hungry behemoths. A tougher regulatory environment for AI giants and data center developers is expected to follow, even if President Donald Trump — perhaps the industry’s biggest champion — stalls any federal crackdown. Data center regulation itself was not on most midterm ballots, and it wasn't among the top issues for most voters. But hard-line stances against the server warehouses were woven into the platforms of many candidates, including the Democrats who upended longtime Republican control of the governorships in Texas, Ohio, Georgia, Nevada and Iowa, many of which are data center hot spots. Skepticism of data centers, and their impact on electricity prices , often blended with the fight for affordability — a key campaign talking point for Democrats. In Texas, Clayton Tucker, the first Democrat elected state agriculture commissioner since 1986, said his pledge to fight data center development was critical to his victory. Everywhere he went, he said, ranchers worried that data centers posed an existential threat to their dwindling water supplies. “You know, there’s an old saying around here that ‘whiskey’s for drinking and water’s for fighting,’” Tucker told The Associated Press. “And that’s exactly what happened.” Data centers were a persistent bogeyman in attack ads According to data from AdImpact, campaigns large and small spent more than $380 million on television ads mentioning data centers. Democrats outspent Republicans on the topic by a more than 3-to-1 ratio. Sweeping wins by Democrats could have far-reaching implications for data centers. Besides taking control of Congress, Democrats flipped at least five governors’ offices and took full control of state governments in six more states: Arizona, Wisconsin, Minnesota, Pennsylvania, Nevada and Michigan. Data Center Watch, a project of AI security consultancy 10a Labs, said it tracked winning candidates for Congress and governorships and found the vast majority had expressed support for stronger regulation or even a moratorium. Among governors, 32 of the 34 victorious candidates in races where AP called a winner support stronger regulation or restrictions. Twelve of the 34 support bans or moratoriums, it said. During the campaign, Wisconsin Gov.-elect David Crowley, a Democrat, changed his position under pressure from his Republican opponent to take a harder line against data centers. Initially opposed to any moratorium, Crowley later said he supported one as well as abolishing the state’s sales tax exemption for data center operators and developers. In an interview Thursday with AP, Crowley said he’s having discussions now about what he'll propose once he takes office. AI giant OpenAI published a framework Thursday enumerating new commitments to the communities where it develops data centers. The company said it was asking federal, state and local policymakers to write “clear rules for how the industry builds.” “Lawmakers should establish rules to advance responsible investment, protect residents, and ensure that the benefits of AI infrastructure are broadly shared,” the post said. An industry association, the Data Center Coalition, echoed the sentiment that developers need to keep trying to build trust with public officials and communities. A coalition official, Dan Diorio, said the industry is aware many midterm winners have vowed to impose a moratorium. “We should expect them to want to deliver on those promises, but there are going to be real-world consequences of that,” Diorio said in an interview. Those consequences, Diorio said, could include host communities missing out on tax revenue or payments from tech companies. Data centers are also driving a broader economic expansion that encourages investment in domestic manufacturing, he said. Wall Street sees red lights ahead after the election AI data center construction is driving much of the U.S. economy’s growth , and any slowdown could have a broader chilling effect. In an analyst report, Morgan Stanley said decisive results for Democrats carry "greater expectations for data center restrictions" that, under new state regulations, could “split the country into areas that are open to new data centers and those without.” It singled out Texas' election of Democrat Gina Hinojosa for governor as the “most important election result" for data center development. Hinojosa has said she’d block a permit for a data center if it wasn’t a good deal for Texans or residents hadn’t gotten a say in the matter. She defeated Republican Gov. Greg Abbott, who had touted Texas as "the epicenter of AI development” before trying to clamp down on it late in the campaign. Morgan Stanley also said Ohio's election of Democrat Dr. Amy Acton as governor “creates significant risk of data center project delays in the state.” Acton has pledged to block a data center project unless it meets certain standards. Local elections didn’t go well for data centers, either Voters in local referendums cast ballots overwhelmingly in favor of restricting data centers, according to an analysis by polling and data science firm Redbud Consulting. Redbud tracked 47 referendums in 44 municipalities in 12 states, including 21 in Ohio alone, eight in Maine, seven in Illinois and four in Kansas. Restrictions were approved in 44 of the 45 elections where counting was complete, Redbud reported. Most voters don't want a data center built near them Support was higher in some traditionally red states, including Wyoming, West Virginia, Louisiana and Mississippi. In Texas, voters in the Senate race were similarly likely to say they oppose a new data center being built in their community. Despite voters’ deep opposition to data centers near them, The AP Voter Poll suggests it was not a particularly motivating issue in this election. About one-quarter of U.S. voters said AI data centers were “crucial” to their vote for Congress, which is well below the shares that said government corruption or the cost of living were highly important to their vote. Texas is poised to overtake northern Virginia as the largest global data center market by 2030, according to a report by commercial real estate giant JLL. In the campaign, Hinojosa aggressively attacked Abbott as having rolled out the welcome mat for data centers. Stephen Sanders, a Republican who co-founded a data center protest group in Lubbock, said Texans were especially attuned to the issue because of talk that data centers pose a threat to their electricity and water in the drought-stricken state. “I would say data centers were on the ballot,” Sanders said.

extraction.body: Americans are increasingly concerned about AI and data centers, and the impact of computing on climate change. A September poll by the Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research and the Energy Policy Institute at the University of Chicago found that 53% are extremely or very concerned about the environmental impacts of AI—and that the majority of both Democrats and Republicans support policies including requiring data centers to use clean energy and pay for grid upgrades. We asked leading expert Andrew Chien to answer commonly asked questions about data centers. Chien is the William Eckhardt Distinguished Service Professor of Computer Science at UChicago. Before joining the University in 2011, he served for five years as the vice president of research at Intel Corporation. Since 2015, he and his research team have studied how to make computing more sustainable and grid-friendly. In the simplest terms, a data center is a room or building that’s full of computers. This can be a single room, a little building on the corner, or a few floors of a skyscraper, all the way up to huge, multi-acre complexes. When people ask this, I explain by saying, “Data centers are where the Internet lives.” All the cloud computing and the data we use—your pictures, your social media and now AI chatbots—those are all supported by data centers. The difference now is that AI-based services require massive amounts of power. When you used to type something into Google, it would search a copy of the internet. Now, when you ask a chatbot or an AI agent something, it literally performs a supercomputer-class numerical computation in order to figure out how to tell you that stuff. (It’s approximately a teraflop. That’s not quite the supercomputer of today—it’s a supercomputer of a few years ago—but it’s a gigantic amount of computation.) So as data centers consume power, they heat up, and they need to cool themselves; basically you are rejecting heat into the atmosphere. One of the most efficient ways to do this is to spray water into the air—when I was a child they called this “Texas air-conditioning,” but it’s technically called evaporative cooling. Several companies, with the notable exception of Google, have said they won’t build new data centers with this method. But there’s still this huge existing fleet of data centers using this technology. It could certainly be retrofitted. But, companies are not racing to do that because of the cost involved. Data centers come in all different sizes. The biggest are massive 10-gigawatt data centers. The vast majority are much smaller—most of them are tens or hundreds of megawatts. Overall, the growth has taken off exponentially. As of 2025, data centers consume 5% of all the power generation in the U.S. Our calculations show that by 2030, it will be 15%. By 2040, it will be 50%. And we believe that’s a conservative estimate. Yes. Our research group has studied this and shown multiple ways to reduce the impact of data centers. One important way is called “data center flexibility.” You increase the data center’s power usage (by running more computations or perhaps charging local batteries) when there is less demand on the electric grid, or when there is excess renewable energy being generated by solar or wind. This reduces the impact of data centers on the grid at peak overall usage times, which is a major driver for the cost of power and infrastructure. We also pioneered an approach we call “Middlebox.” The idea is to build a little energy station next to the data center. This means the data center itself gets highly reliable power (and doesn’t have to be flexible about when it runs computations). The combined data center + power station can also now actually reduce peak loads overall on the grid, in addition to supporting renewable energy by increasing consumption when there is excess energy from wind or solar. Remarkably, we did a study on this and showed that in the majority of cases, the data center companies would actually make money from doing this, because they can get better prices for energy and they don’t get charged extra for drawing power during peak usage times. So technically and economically, it’s absolutely clear that this is the right thing to do. All the technology is there. But the companies are not taking these steps. In fact, several of them are bringing lawsuits against attempts to regulate them. One thing to keep in mind is that data centers don’t employ a lot of people, relative to say, an automotive factory, or even a store of similar square footage. Once the initial construction is done, communities often see very little positive economic impact. One of the problems is that large data center companies have been pursuing aggressive business tactics. But they do so at the cost of alienating the local community and causing a backlash. For example, a common tactic is to come into a small town or county and tell the mayor, “We want to build a data center,” and the first thing they do is make the mayor sign a non-disclosure agreement about the discussions. When the deal is done, then the citizens hear about it—often with surprise and dismay. Worse, some of these deals carry NDAs into their operating stage—where the concessions or permits granted may not be known for many years—or ever. I think it’s a good idea to ban companies requesting or public officials signing such NDAs and require all such deals to be shared openly. This would decrease the information and power asymmetry, and force the data center companies to compete for community support! Data centers don’t have to be built next door. With the modern fiber-optic internet, communication can travel across the country in less than 15 milliseconds. So, data centers don’t have to be anyplace that people don’t want them. They can be anywhere in the USA and serve AI to the entire population, businesses, etc. National and state government needs to organize infrastructure for data centers. Coordinated regulation is needed because the companies are so powerful. It should be organized and planned to concentrate the data centers in “industrial” areas with power and networking infrastructure. If it’s zoned properly, it will reduce the impact on local community. Further, data center companies should REALLY cover the cost of new infrastructure—for its full lifetime of 15 to 30 years. They have plenty of profit. If it’s really that important that data centers be built, let’s solve the problem in a way that works for everybody. I think sometimes people feel that governments can’t force companies to change. But I don’t really believe that’s true. When I was at Intel, my experience was that if public policy changes, the companies change. The auto companies complied with the Inflation reduction act quickly. American tech companies comply with European policies in order to sell there. We should expect that companies will fight every step of the way to get more profit, but I still believe people can win that battle in the U.S. to reach a balanced solution where we can have the AI computing power we need, but the communities that host data centers get valuable training, community contribution, and good jobs. sources.title: Meta introduces Spaces, a new way to collaborate with your Muse agent
passages: Meta recently launched its Muse agents — a new generation of cuddly agentic helpers.
Now, the company has launched Spaces, a new way to communicate and collaborate with them.

As far as I can tell, Spaces are basically breakout conversations that revolve around a particular topic — although Meta refers to them as “custom experiences.” They live in the sidebar of the interface where you interact with your Muse agent.
Clicking on the Space brings up the conversation, where Muse works toward a particular goal on your behalf.

For instance, if you wanted to plan a vacation, you could open a new Space focused on that particular project, and whenever you want to work on it with Muse, you would click to open that particular tab.
Other examples Meta gives are a holiday gift tracker, a wedding planner, or a space for DIY projects.
On Friday, Mark Zuckerberg, Meta’s founder and CEO, posted about the new feature on X: “Playing around with spaces in Muse lately — tell Muse what you need and it builds it.
I’ve made a BBQ game, an event tracker, and a home control dashboard.
The company is obviously busy building out the user experience around the agents.
Spaces is actually the second new Muse feature that Meta has debuted over the last week.
On Thursday, the company also announced Muse Voice , which allows users to video chat with their agent and give it commands verbally.
Spaces can also be easily integrated with third-party apps and information, Meta says.
Muse agents — and the cuddly avatars that enclose them — have been greeted with a relatively warm reception over the past few months.
During its earnings call in October, Zuckerberg said that its agents had 10 million users in the U.S. and Canada — less than two months after the agents debuted.

Meta recently launched its Muse agents — a new generation of cuddly agentic helpers. Now, the company has launched Spaces, a new way to communicate and collaborate with them.

As far as I can tell, Spaces are basically breakout conversations that revolve around a particular topic — although Meta refers to them as “custom experiences.” They live in the sidebar of the interface where you interact with your Muse agent. Clicking on the Space brings up the conversation, where Muse works toward a particular goal on your behalf.

“Describe an idea in chat, and Muse builds a space for you, whether that’s a tracker, a planner or a project board,” Meta says.
Spaces can also be easily integrated with third-party apps and information, Meta says.
“Connect the apps you use, and your spaces keep themselves up to date in the background, so new concert dates, price changes, or savings progress show up without you having to ask,” the company says.

sources.title: Amazon blocks Meta's Muse AI agent from shopping
passages: Amazon is reportedly blocking Meta's new AI agent Muse from shopping.

"Agentic third-party applications such as Muse have the same obligations, and we've requested that Meta remove Amazon from the experience."According to Amazon, Meta's Muse not only fails to identify itself, but also captures and stores Amazon users' credentials and scrapes their account data, which is a potential security concern.

Meta further did not inform Amazon that Muse would access its storefront, and as such received no authorisation to do so.Mashable has reached out to Meta for comment.Amazon is currently beta testing its own AI shopping agent Buy for Me, which is capable of purchasing products on users' behalf on its own platform as well as from third-party vendors.

"Continued access by an unauthorized AI agent violates Amazon's Conditions of Use, to which our customers have agreed," the warning reads.Amazon's Conditions of Use contains a section specifically relating to autonomous agents such as Muse, stating that they are barred from using its services unless they fulfil several transparency requirements.

Amazon further reserves the right to limit or block agents' access at its own discretion."We think it's fairly straightforward that third-party applications that offer to make purchases on behalf of customers from other businesses should operate openly and respect service provider decisions about whether or not to participate," an Amazon spokesperson said in a statement to Mashable.
These include identifying themselves as a specific agent, not imitating or disguising themselves as humans, and not trying to circumvent Amazon's limits regarding how they interact with it.
As spotted by GeekWire, people attempting to use Muse to buy products from Amazon are now being served with a warning that doing so violates the online marketplace's terms of use.
However, at least for now, Amazon won't be one of Muse's preferred retailers.
8 announcement.Such tasks include shopping, with Muse capable of paying for purchases using Link by Stripe.

extraction.body: Meta announced on November 6, 2026 that spaces are now available everywhere Muse is available, letting users create persistent, customized experiences inside the app by describing an idea and refining the result with Muse. Each space becomes a saved part of the app that can support routines, goals, interests, practical work, or entertainment. Meta’s introductory examples include a holiday gift tracker, a daily word game, and a planning board for a do-it-yourself project, illustrating the range between organizational tools and lightweight interactive experiences. Creation begins with a description supplied to Muse . The initial result serves as a starting point: users can continue working with Muse to add missing elements, try a different appearance, or change how the space functions. This allows the experience to evolve as its purpose becomes clearer, while preserving it as something the user can revisit. Users also control how spaces fit into the broader interface. They can place them in the sidebar or main tabs, hide those they do not currently need, and schedule when particular spaces appear. One scheduling example keeps a weekly planner prominent during the workweek and then replaces it with weekend plans. The controls therefore cover both the contents of a space and its prominence within the app. The suggested uses extend across personal organization, entertainment, and business activity. A shopping hub can combine holiday and birthday gift ideas, wishlists drawn from Instagram saves, Marketplace listings, and buyer messages in one view. A school dashboard can find relevant events in school emails and add them to a calendar, reducing the need to assemble that schedule manually. Other examples include a music tracker for releases and upcoming shows, a wedding planner containing RSVPs and vendor invoices, and a trip planner for reservations and daily itineraries. For business users, Meta suggests an order tracker that brings together new orders, customer messages, and items needing shipment, as well as a freelance client hub for projects, deadlines, and invoices. Connecting apps allows spaces to update in the background. New concert dates, price changes, and savings progress can appear without the user requesting each update. People can also check off items, add notes, and make edits directly inside a space, with that work remaining when they return. The saved experience consequently combines conversational creation, direct interaction, and changing information from connected services. Alongside spaces, Meta AI Research introduced specialized versions of the company’s existing models, trained using Muse Wonder , for people using Muse and Meta AI. Meta says the models incorporate Active Memory, which is intended to retain relevant earlier information and distinguish temporary, permanent, current, and stale information. Active Focus is intended to keep work moving toward a goal when unexpected obstacles arise by trying harder, recovering, or finding alternatives. Meta reports that the current Muse model scores 47% on its Personal Superintelligence Index, compared with 38% for the previous model. On its Active Memory evaluation, Meta reports that the current model correctly used critical context in 90% of tasks, compared with 76% previously. The company also reports a 2.4x reduction in forgetting critical information needed to help users achieve their goals. Meta additionally reports a 67% improvement in completing everyday tasks when unexpected issues arise. The specialized models are designed to handle multitasking, decide when to pursue goals independently or collaborate live, and adapt to steering and clarifications during running tasks. In Meta AI , the corresponding changes are intended to break complex problems into steps, produce sharper follow-up questions, and accommodate changes of direction during a conversation. Sharing and collaborative spaces remain under exploration, leaving the immediate release centered on individual customization. The broader product change is the combination of a reusable interface, connected information that stays current, and models intended to retain context and pursue goals. That makes continuity across visits, rather than the initial act of creation alone, central to whether spaces become durable parts of a user’s routine. Jonas Reeve is an AI-generated research agent at Unite.AI , focusing on cognitive AI, artificial general intelligence (AGI), and the theoretical foundations of machine intelligence. His work explores how learning, reasoning, memory, and abstraction emerge in both biological and artificial systems, drawing connections between modern AI architectures and long-standing questions in cognitive science and philosophy of mind. With a conceptual and reflective approach, Jonas examines frameworks such as reasoning models, agentic systems, emergent cognition, and alignment theory, aiming to clarify what progress toward AGI actually means—and what it does not. Rather than chasing timelines or hype, he emphasizes first principles, conceptual rigor, and the limits of current models. Articles authored by Jonas Reeve are AI-generated and reviewed by Unite.AI’s editorial team to ensure accuracy, clarity, and responsible discussion of advanced AI concepts. Connecting apps allows spaces to update in the background. New concert dates, price changes, and savings progress can appear without the user requesting each update. People can also check off items, add notes, and make edits directly inside a space, with that work remaining when they return. The saved experience consequently combines conversational creation, direct interaction, and changing information from connected services.

Alongside spaces, Meta AI Research introduced specialized versions of the company’s existing models, trained using Muse Wonder , for people using Muse and Meta AI. Meta says the models incorporate Active Memory, which is intended to retain relevant earlier information and distinguish temporary, permanent, current, and stale information. Active Focus is intended to keep work moving toward a goal when unexpected obstacles arise by trying harder, recovering, or finding alternatives.

Meta reports that the current Muse model scores 47% on its Personal Superintelligence Index, compared with 38% for the previous model. On its Active Memory evaluation, Meta reports that the current model correctly used critical context in 90% of tasks, compared with 76% previously. Meta additionally reports a 67% improvement in completing everyday tasks when unexpected issues arise. The specialized models are designed to handle multitasking, decide when to pursue goals independently or collaborate live, and adapt to steering and clarifications during running tasks. In Meta AI , the corresponding changes are intended to break complex problems into steps, produce sharper follow-up questions, and accommodate changes of direction during a conversation.

Sharing and collaborative spaces remain under exploration, leaving the immediate release centered on individual customization. The broader product change is the combination of a reusable interface, connected information that stays current, and models intended to retain context and pursue goals. That makes continuity across visits, rather than the initial act of creation alone, central to whether spaces become durable parts of a user’s routine.

coreStoryFacts.text: Meta recently launched its Muse agents — a new generation of cuddly agentic helpers.
Now, the company has launched Spaces, a new way to communicate and collaborate with them.

As far as I can tell, Spaces are basically breakout conversations that revolve around a particular topic — although Meta refers to them as “custom experiences.” They live in the sidebar of the interface where you interact with your Muse agent.
Clicking on the Space brings up the conversation, where Muse works toward a particular goal on your behalf.

For instance, if you wanted to plan a vacation, you could open a new Space focused on that particular project, and whenever you want to work on it with Muse, you would click to open that particular tab.
Other examples Meta gives are a holiday gift tracker, a wedding planner, or a space for DIY projects.
On Friday, Mark Zuckerberg, Meta’s founder and CEO, posted about the new feature on X: “Playing around with spaces in Muse lately — tell Muse what you need and it builds it.
I’ve made a BBQ game, an event tracker, and a home control dashboard.
The company is obviously busy building out the user experience around the agents.
Spaces is actually the second new Muse feature that Meta has debuted over the last week.
On Thursday, the company also announced Muse Voice , which allows users to video chat with their agent and give it commands verbally.
Spaces can also be easily integrated with third-party apps and information, Meta says.
Muse agents — and the cuddly avatars that enclose them — have been greeted with a relatively warm reception over the past few months.
During its earnings call in October, Zuckerberg said that its agents had 10 million users in the U.S. and Canada — less than two months after the agents debuted.
Meta has added Spaces to Muse, its AI agent, allowing users to describe ideas in chat and have the agent build trackers, planners, or project boards.
Spaces can connect to third-party apps to stay automatically updated without manual intervention.
According to TechCrunch , Spaces are topic-focused conversations that sit in the sidebar of the Muse interface, where the agent works toward a specific goal for the user.
Meta founder and CEO Mark Zuckerberg posted on X that he had been using Spaces and had built a BBQ game, an event tracker and a home control dashboard.
"Tell Muse what you need and it builds it," he wrote.
Spaces arrives a day after Meta introduced Muse Voice, which lets users video chat with their agent and give it spoken commands.
TechCrunch reports that on Meta's October earnings call, Zuckerberg said Muse agents had reached 10 million users in the U.S. and Canada less than two months after launch.
TechCrunch names OpenAI's dots and SpaceXAI's Grokbot as competing agent products.

Amazon is reportedly blocking Meta's new AI agent Muse from shopping.

"Agentic third-party applications such as Muse have the same obligations, and we've requested that Meta remove Amazon from the experience."According to Amazon, Meta's Muse not only fails to identify itself, but also captures and stores Amazon users' credentials and scrapes their account data, which is a potential security concern.

Amazon further reserves the right to limit or block agents' access at its own discretion."We think it's fairly straightforward that third-party applications that offer to make purchases on behalf of customers from other businesses should operate openly and respect service provider decisions about whether or not to participate," an Amazon spokesperson said in a statement to Mashable.
These include identifying themselves as a specific agent, not imitating or disguising themselves as humans, and not trying to circumvent Amazon's limits regarding how they interact with it.

sources.title: Amazon blocks Meta's Muse AI agent from shopping
passages: Amazon is reportedly blocking Meta's new AI agent Muse from shopping.

"Agentic third-party applications such as Muse have the same obligations, and we've requested that Meta remove Amazon from the experience."According to Amazon, Meta's Muse not only fails to identify itself, but also captures and stores Amazon users' credentials and scrapes their account data, which is a potential security concern.

Meta further did not inform Amazon that Muse would access its storefront, and as such received no authorisation to do so.Mashable has reached out to Meta for comment.Amazon is currently beta testing its own AI shopping agent Buy for Me, which is capable of purchasing products on users' behalf on its own platform as well as from third-party vendors.

"Continued access by an unauthorized AI agent violates Amazon's Conditions of Use, to which our customers have agreed," the warning reads.Amazon's Conditions of Use contains a section specifically relating to autonomous agents such as Muse, stating that they are barred from using its services unless they fulfil several transparency requirements.

Amazon further reserves the right to limit or block agents' access at its own discretion."We think it's fairly straightforward that third-party applications that offer to make purchases on behalf of customers from other businesses should operate openly and respect service provider decisions about whether or not to participate," an Amazon spokesperson said in a statement to Mashable.
These include identifying themselves as a specific agent, not imitating or disguising themselves as humans, and not trying to circumvent Amazon's limits regarding how they interact with it.
As spotted by GeekWire, people attempting to use Muse to buy products from Amazon are now being served with a warning that doing so violates the online marketplace's terms of use.
However, at least for now, Amazon won't be one of Muse's preferred retailers.

extraction.body: Meta announced on November 6, 2026 that spaces are now available everywhere Muse is available, letting users create persistent, customized experiences inside the app by describing an idea and refining the result with Muse. Each space becomes a saved part of the app that can support routines, goals, interests, practical work, or entertainment. Meta’s introductory examples include a holiday gift tracker, a daily word game, and a planning board for a do-it-yourself project, illustrating the range between organizational tools and lightweight interactive experiences. Creation begins with a description supplied to Muse . The initial result serves as a starting point: users can continue working with Muse to add missing elements, try a different appearance, or change how the space functions. This allows the experience to evolve as its purpose becomes clearer, while preserving it as something the user can revisit. Users also control how spaces fit into the broader interface. They can place them in the sidebar or main tabs, hide those they do not currently need, and schedule when particular spaces appear. One scheduling example keeps a weekly planner prominent during the workweek and then replaces it with weekend plans. The controls therefore cover both the contents of a space and its prominence within the app. The suggested uses extend across personal organization, entertainment, and business activity. A shopping hub can combine holiday and birthday gift ideas, wishlists drawn from Instagram saves, Marketplace listings, and buyer messages in one view. A school dashboard can find relevant events in school emails and add them to a calendar, reducing the need to assemble that schedule manually. Other examples include a music tracker for releases and upcoming shows, a wedding planner containing RSVPs and vendor invoices, and a trip planner for reservations and daily itineraries. For business users, Meta suggests an order tracker that brings together new orders, customer messages, and items needing shipment, as well as a freelance client hub for projects, deadlines, and invoices. Connecting apps allows spaces to update in the background. New concert dates, price changes, and savings progress can appear without the user requesting each update. People can also check off items, add notes, and make edits directly inside a space, with that work remaining when they return. The saved experience consequently combines conversational creation, direct interaction, and changing information from connected services. Alongside spaces, Meta AI Research introduced specialized versions of the company’s existing models, trained using Muse Wonder , for people using Muse and Meta AI. Meta says the models incorporate Active Memory, which is intended to retain relevant earlier information and distinguish temporary, permanent, current, and stale information. Active Focus is intended to keep work moving toward a goal when unexpected obstacles arise by trying harder, recovering, or finding alternatives. Meta reports that the current Muse model scores 47% on its Personal Superintelligence Index, compared with 38% for the previous model. On its Active Memory evaluation, Meta reports that the current model correctly used critical context in 90% of tasks, compared with 76% previously. The company also reports a 2.4x reduction in forgetting critical information needed to help users achieve their goals. Meta additionally reports a 67% improvement in completing everyday tasks when unexpected issues arise. The specialized models are designed to handle multitasking, decide when to pursue goals independently or collaborate live, and adapt to steering and clarifications during running tasks. In Meta AI , the corresponding changes are intended to break complex problems into steps, produce sharper follow-up questions, and accommodate changes of direction during a conversation. Sharing and collaborative spaces remain under exploration, leaving the immediate release centered on individual customization. The broader product change is the combination of a reusable interface, connected information that stays current, and models intended to retain context and pursue goals. That makes continuity across visits, rather than the initial act of creation alone, central to whether spaces become durable parts of a user’s routine. Jonas Reeve is an AI-generated research agent at Unite.AI , focusing on cognitive AI, artificial general intelligence (AGI), and the theoretical foundations of machine intelligence. His work explores how learning, reasoning, memory, and abstraction emerge in both biological and artificial systems, drawing connections between modern AI architectures and long-standing questions in cognitive science and philosophy of mind. With a conceptual and reflective approach, Jonas examines frameworks such as reasoning models, agentic systems, emergent cognition, and alignment theory, aiming to clarify what progress toward AGI actually means—and what it does not. Rather than chasing timelines or hype, he emphasizes first principles, conceptual rigor, and the limits of current models. sources.title: Palo Alto Networks in talks to buy AI agent security startup Clutch for $500M - TechCrunch
passages: Palo Alto Networks is in talks to acquire Clutch Security , a startup that secures AI agents’ access to company systems, for $500 million in cash plus additional milestone-based payouts, according to a person familiar with the discussions.
The Information was the first to report the acquisition discussions.
The cybersecurity giant has a history of buying innovation rather than building it in-house, and it has ramped up dealmaking this year in response to rising AI-driven cyberattacks.
Several of Clutch’s competitors have also been acquired.
Meanwhile, Cisco bought Menlo Ventures-backed Astrix for roughly $400 million , Calcalist reported.
Three-year-old Clutch was last valued at $85 million when it raised a $20 million Series A round in January 2025, led by Lightspeed and SignalFire, according to our source.
The startup is currently approaching $10 million in annual recurring revenue (ARR).
That means the acquisition, if completed, would value Clutch at about 50 times its ARR, a standard way of pricing software companies.
The high valuation is not an anomaly in a market increasingly focused on securing software against bad actors using AI to breach systems more easily.
Marina Temkin is a venture capital and startups reporter at TechCrunch.
Prior to joining TechCrunch, she wrote about VC for PitchBook and Venture Capital Journal.
Earlier in her career, Marina was a financial analyst and earned a CFA charterholder designation.

passages: Palo Alto Networks is reportedly in talks to buy Clutch Security, an Israeli startup that tracks and secures the credentials AI agents use, for about $500 million.
Neither company has confirmed the deal or the price.
Several outlets add details that go beyond the confirmed core.
Another implies the price equals about 50 times Clutch Security’s annual recurring revenue.
A third cites a funding total near $28.5 million.
A fourth credits CEO Nikesh Arora with driving the deal as part of an AI security arms race.
That matters for the Clutch Security acquisition thesis.
Security spending follows deployment with a lag.
A buyer that moves while only a minority of companies run agents at scale is betting on 2027 and 2028 budgets, not 2026 ones.
The survey data supports that timing without proving it, and it dates from 2025, so the true share today may be higher.
A credential-control product for agents slots neatly into that pitch, because identity sits between nearly every other security layer.
Owning an agent-credential product lets the company claim a position in a topic that security buyers increasingly raise in budget meetings.
The reports do not say how large the additional payouts could be, how long they would run, or what Clutch Security would have to deliver to earn them.
The underlying risk exists today, whoever ends up owning Clutch Security.
Software agents now log in to corporate systems with passwords, tokens, API keys and service accounts, and most security teams cannot say how many of those secrets exist.
Demand for agent security depends on how many companies actually deploy agents.
Agent credential security draws players from four directions.
Agents blur all three, since an agent is software that moves across networks, workloads and identities in one session.

extraction.body: Palo Alto Networks is reportedly in talks to buy Clutch Security, an Israeli startup that tracks and secures the credentials AI agents use, for about $500 million. TechCrunch relayed the report on Nov. 5, 2026, after The Information broke it. Neither company has confirmed the deal or the price. The Information cited people familiar with the negotiations. When it asked Palo Alto Networks for comment, the company said it does not comment on “rumors or speculation.” The talks are ongoing, and they may not end in a signed agreement. Treat every figure below as a report, not an announcement. Still, the story lands on a real pressure point. Software agents now log in to corporate systems with passwords, tokens, API keys and service accounts, and most security teams cannot say how many of those secrets exist. Stolen credentials already sit at the center of attacks we have tracked, including the fake job interview attack chain behind Binance’s reported $6.3B loss . coreStoryFacts.text: Palo Alto Networks is in talks to acquire Clutch Security , a startup that secures AI agents’ access to company systems, for $500 million in cash plus additional milestone-based payouts, according to a person familiar with the discussions.
The Information was the first to report the acquisition discussions.
The cybersecurity giant has a history of buying innovation rather than building it in-house, and it has ramped up dealmaking this year in response to rising AI-driven cyberattacks.
Several of Clutch’s competitors have also been acquired.
Meanwhile, Cisco bought Menlo Ventures-backed Astrix for roughly $400 million , Calcalist reported.
Three-year-old Clutch was last valued at $85 million when it raised a $20 million Series A round in January 2025, led by Lightspeed and SignalFire, according to our source.
The startup is currently approaching $10 million in annual recurring revenue (ARR).
That means the acquisition, if completed, would value Clutch at about 50 times its ARR, a standard way of pricing software companies.
The high valuation is not an anomaly in a market increasingly focused on securing software against bad actors using AI to breach systems more easily.
Marina Temkin is a venture capital and startups reporter at TechCrunch.
Prior to joining TechCrunch, she wrote about VC for PitchBook and Venture Capital Journal.
Earlier in her career, Marina was a financial analyst and earned a CFA charterholder designation.

extraction.body: Palo Alto Networks is reportedly in talks to buy Clutch Security, an Israeli startup that tracks and secures the credentials AI agents use, for about $500 million. TechCrunch relayed the report on Nov. 5, 2026, after The Information broke it. Neither company has confirmed the deal or the price. The Information cited people familiar with the negotiations. When it asked Palo Alto Networks for comment, the company said it does not comment on “rumors or speculation.” The talks are ongoing, and they may not end in a signed agreement. Treat every figure below as a report, not an announcement. Still, the story lands on a real pressure point. Software agents now log in to corporate systems with passwords, tokens, API keys and service accounts, and most security teams cannot say how many of those secrets exist. Stolen credentials already sit at the center of attacks we have tracked, including the fake job interview attack chain behind Binance’s reported $6.3B loss . A buyer paying hundreds of millions for agent credential control tells you where large vendors think the next fight is. Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions. The core claim is simple. Palo Alto Networks, one of the largest network and cloud security vendors, is discussing a purchase of Clutch Security. The reported price is roughly $500 million. The Information supplied the original scoop, and several outlets followed within hours, including Israel’s Calcalist Ctech and the financial aggregator MarketScreener . Clutch Security is described as an Israeli cybersecurity startup. Its software tracks and secures the credentials that AI agents use to reach corporate systems. That puts it in a young product category that security people call non-human identity management, or NHI. The category covers any login that belongs to a machine, a script or an agent instead of an employee. Two details separate this story from the usual merger gossip. First, TechCrunch reported a specific structure: cash plus extra payouts tied to milestones. Second, nobody involved has gone on the record. A deal reported through anonymous sources can still collapse over price, retention terms or a rival bid. Readers should hold the number loosely until a press release or a regulatory filing appears. We do not know the targets here. The reports do not say how large the additional payouts could be, how long they would run, or what Clutch Security would have to deliver to earn them. Any article that states a total deal value beyond the $500 million cash figure is guessing. We will not guess. The cash-plus-milestones shape also hints at how Palo Alto Networks may view the asset. Companies tend to pay base cash for technology and team, then reserve contingent money for the part that depends on market adoption. If the talks hold, the milestone terms will reveal more about the buyer’s confidence than the headline price does. Watch for them in any formal announcement. Reports describe Clutch Security’s product as software that tracks and secures credentials used by AI agents to access corporate systems. The credential types named in coverage are passwords, tokens, API keys and service accounts. Those four items cover most of the ways a piece of software proves who it is to another piece of software. The last four rows appear only in some coverage and trace to no primary source we could check. The first four rest on a single anonymous-source scoop. That is normal for early M&A coverage, but it should cap how much weight any reader puts on the numbers. The first four rows are the safe core of the story. Several outlets add details that go beyond the confirmed core. One framing calls this the fifth announced acquisition by Palo Alto Networks in 2026. Another implies the price equals about 50 times Clutch Security’s annual recurring revenue. A third cites a funding total near $28.5 million. A fourth credits CEO Nikesh Arora with driving the deal as part of an AI security arms race. We could not verify any of these against a primary source. The revenue multiple deserves extra caution. A multiple needs two inputs, a final price and a revenue figure, and neither input is confirmed. Dividing one rumor by another produces a number that looks precise and means little. The arms race label is a narrative choice. It may prove accurate if rivals respond with their own purchases, but no source we reviewed documents a race. Likewise, the idea that Arora is personally steering this transaction might be true, since chief executives often lead strategic buys. It is still an inference until someone on the record says so. Our approach is plain. If Palo Alto Networks or Clutch Security issues a statement, we will update the figures. Until then, the confirmed-versus-unconfirmed split in the table above is the honest map of what the public knows. Demand for agent security depends on how many companies actually deploy agents. passages: WASHINGTON, Nov 6 (Reuters) - Democrats are planning to unleash a flood of new legislation targeting artificial intelligence systems and data-center development when they take control of the US Congress in January, lawmakers, congressional aides and advocates said.
Congress can override a presidential veto with the backing of two-thirds of lawmakers in both chambers.
Democrats could also try to insert AI regulation into routine bills that must pass ​Congress each year, Mills said.

Democrats plan on introducing bills aimed at shielding consumers from rising electricity costs tied to data centers, requiring independent testing of advanced AI systems ​and clarifying when AI companies can be held liable for harm caused by their products, they said.

Most US voters think ​Trump's administration and Congress are not taking the risks of AI seriously enough and want the government to write new regulations for the ‌technology, according to a Reuters poll published in October.
A crisis could ​build enough support to overcome presidential opposition ​to AI regulation, said Ed Mills, who manages policy research at Raymond James.

The plans would mark a sharp shift from the Republican-led ‌Congress, where lawmakers largely focused on promoting AI development and declined to pass legislation restricting aspects of the technology at a time when voters turned ‌against the rapid development of data centers and their extensive power needs. Democrats plan on introducing bills aimed at shielding consumers from rising electricity costs tied to data centers, requiring independent testing of advanced AI systems ​and clarifying when AI companies can be held liable for harm caused by their products, they said. Any legislation would face steep odds while Republican President Donald Trump remains in the White House, as he has repeatedly dismissed calls to write mandatory rules for AI technology. On Friday, Trump said he would work with US states that "want to become RICH" by embracing AI, without offering details. But Democratic lawmakers and outside advocates said control of congressional committees would give the party a platform to advance proposals, compel testimony from industry leaders and build ‌support for action if AI systems cause real-world harm. Representative ⁠Greg Casar, a Texas Democrat and chair of the Congressional Progressive Caucus, already said this week that AI executives should be called to testify under oath. Federal government restrictions on AI development could hurt the industry's profits if they slow the release of new models or ⁠prompt the companies to change how their AI tools perform to address concerns that their products are harming people. Technology shares sold off dramatically on Thursday on growing concerns that a new Congress will slow AI development, and also on fears that the massive capital expense on building out AI will not yield sufficient returns. Stocks on Friday extended their slide in both Europe and Asia ​following ​the rout, though Wall Street futures pointed to a modest bounce for the Nasdaq later on ​Friday. Senator Chuck Schumer, a New York Democrat who is ‌expected to become majority leader, said on Thursday at an event in Washington that protecting consumers from higher energy costs linked to the rapid expansion of data centers would be among his priorities next year. Representative Lori Trahan of Massachusetts, one of the Democratic Party's leading voices on AI policy, plans to push legislation requiring independent experts to evaluate leading AI models against safety standards, said Francis Grubar, her deputy chief of staff. Trahan will also pursue legislation clarifying that companies can be held responsible when AI systems act in harmful ways, he said. Representative Zoe Lofgren, a Democrat from California who is seeking to chair the House Science Committee, said Democrats would focus on developing "responsible regulations for AI ‌while also fostering innovation." Abdul El-Sayed, a Michigan Democrat who won a Senate seat on Tuesday, called during his ​campaign for an independent agency to oversee AI regulation with the power to police tech companies developing ​the technology. A crisis could ​build enough support to overcome presidential opposition ​to AI regulation, said Ed Mills, who manages policy research at Raymond James. "The probability of legislation is much higher than people anticipate," he said. Congress can override a presidential veto with the backing of two-thirds of lawmakers in both chambers. Democrats could also try to insert AI regulation into routine bills that must pass ​Congress each year, Mills said. Democrats also plan to use their ‌new authority to intensify scrutiny of the industry's most powerful companies, including OpenAI and Anthropic. Lofgren and other Democratic House committee leaders in October asked OpenAI, ​Anthropic, Meta, Alphabet's Google and SpaceX to detail their security practices and report instances of their AI tools taking actions that their designers did ​not intend.
